strengths: Insightful and well-motivated empirical study: The paper provides a clear and compelling analysis distinguishing the behavior of attention sinks in vision transformers from large language models. The explanation that ViTs require early layers to identify semantically uninformative patches (supported by foreground/background experiments in Fig. 3 and the comparison with pretrained registers in Fig. 7) is conceptually neat and illuminating.

Effective and training-free plug-in design: RegCache operates without model retraining and can be layered on top of multiple existing PTQ algorithms (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, QuaRot), providing substantial and consistent performance gains, particularly in challenging low-precision settings such as W6A6 and W4A4.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is benchmarked across five major vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2) over zero-shot classification across diverse datasets (ImageNet-1k, Stanford Cars, Flowers-102, Food-101, CIFAR-100) and zero-shot image-text retrieval on MS-COCO.

Thorough ablation and analysis: The paper includes meaningful ablations isolating the roles of prefix caching versus token deletion (Tab. 6), runtime and FLOPs overhead analysis (Tab. 12), and visualizations of the identified register tokens.
weaknesses: Model size diversity: The experiments focus predominantly on ViT-Base architectures (CLIP-B/16, OpenCLIP-B/16, SigLIP-B/16, DINOv2-B/14). Outliers in transformers tend to worsen significantly as model scale increases to Large and Huge; evaluating on ViT-L or ViT-H would have strengthened the empirical claims.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and manual heuristics: The method introduces several search parameters (the number of register copies $\tau$, candidate pool size $k$, number of deleted tokens $\tilde{k}$, and the range of layers where prefixes are applied). Furthermore, DINOv2 required a different prefix insertion strategy (only at the sensitive layer rather than propagated forward), highlighting some ad-hoc tuning per architecture family.

Applicability to dense visual tasks: The inference step explicitly deletes tokens with extreme activation norms, which alters the regular 2D spatial grid. While pool-based zero-shot classification and global retrieval are unaffected, this may cause complications or spatial distortion if applied to downstream dense tasks such as object detection, segmentation, or spatial grounding.

strengths: The paper provides a compelling and insightful bridge between the recent discovery of vision transformer registers / attention sinks and post-training activation quantization.

The empirical investigation explaining why outliers emerge specifically in middle layers (rather than early layers as in LLMs) is well-motivated and convincingly validated through foreground/background masking experiments and comparison with register-trained models.
The finding that middle-layer outlier tokens have very high cross-image cosine similarity (~0.89) provides a solid justification for caching and reusing pre-computed universal registers.

RegCache is training-free, lightweight, and serves as an effective plug-in method on top of existing PTQ techniques (e.g., PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q), yielding substantial accuracy improvements especially under challenging low-bit regimes (W6A6, W4A4).

The paper is clearly written, logically organized, and includes comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2), zero-shot benchmarks, retrieval tasks, and ablation studies.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted exclusively to Base-scale models (ViT-B/16, ViT-B/14). Evaluating scalability on smaller (ViT-S/ViT-T) or larger variants (ViT-L/ViT-H) would help confirm whether the intermediate-layer outlier dynamics and register caching generalizability hold universally across model depths and capacities.

The framework relies on several sensitive hyperparameters—such as the number of prefix copies $\tau$, candidate pool size $k$, and the number of deleted tokens $\tilde{k}$—which are searched via heuristics on a reference dataset. A systematic sensitivity analysis demonstrating the stability of performance across these hyperparameter choices is lacking.

Heuristic differences are required across model families; for instance, CLIP and SigLIP insert prefixes from the sensitive layer up to the final layer, whereas DINOv2 requires prefixing only at a single layer. A more unified or automated layer-selection criterion would make the method easier to deploy out-of-the-box.

strengths: Insightful analysis of outlier emergence in vision transformers: The paper provides a clear conceptual and empirical distinction between LLMs and ViTs. Specifically, it convincingly demonstrates why outliers emerge in intermediate layers rather than early layers in vision encoders (because early layers are needed to identify semantically uninformative patches), supported by the foreground/background isolation experiment on ImageNet-9.

Effective and training-free plug-in formulation: RegCache operates without model fine-tuning or retraining. It successfully bridges attention-sink/register concepts with PTQ by caching universal middle-layer registers and deleting residual outlier tokens at inference time.

Extensive empirical evaluation across models and tasks: The method is validated on five diverse vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2) across multiple benchmarks (ImageNet-1k, MS-COCO retrieval, four transfer datasets) and quantization regimes (W8A8, W6A6, W4A4, and weight-only AWQ).

Orthogonality and strong gains with existing PTQ baselines: RegCache consistently boosts existing state-of-the-art PTQ methods (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, QuaRot), achieving substantial accuracy recovery especially under aggressive low-bit activations (W6A6 and W4A4).
weaknesses: Heuristic hyperparameter search and model-specific tuning: As acknowledged by the authors, the pipeline introduces multiple hyperparameters (candidate pool size k, prefix copy count τ, number of deleted tokens k̃, and layer selection) that must be searched using a calibration split. Notably, DINOv2 requires a different prefix insertion strategy (only at the searched layer) compared to CLIP/SigLIP, indicating that the framework is not yet fully automated across different pretraining paradigms.

Evaluation restricted primarily to Base-scale encoders: Experiments are almost entirely limited to ViT-Base architectures (e.g., CLIP-B/16, SigLIP-B/16). Validating whether the middle-layer register behavior and quantization recovery scale consistently to ViT-Large (ViT-L/14) or ViT-Giant would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Lack of evaluation on dense vision tasks: The inference pipeline deletes top-k̃ patch tokens. While discarding uninformative background patches does not harm (and can even help) global classification and image-text retrieval, deleting tokens could disrupt spatial coordinate alignment required for dense downstream tasks such as object detection, segmentation, or open-vocabulary localization.

Hardware latency overhead in non-autoregressive models: While the FLOP overhead is minimal (<0.2%), Table 12 reveals a ~5% wall-clock latency increase on CLIP and OpenCLIP due to sequence modification and KV-cache handling, which can be non-trivial for low-latency edge deployment.

strengths: Insightful Analysis of ViT Outliers: The paper provides a clear empirical explanation of why activation outliers emerge in intermediate/middle layers of vision encoders rather than in early layers (as observed in LLMs), demonstrating that continuous tokenization requires several layers before semantically uninformative background patches are identified as attention sinks.

Effective, Training-Free Plug-in Formulation: RegCache is simple, training-free, and lightweight. It acts as an orthogonal plug-in module that can be stacked on top of existing PTQ methods (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, ERQ) with minimal inference latency overhead (<1.5% in TensorRT profiling).

Comprehensive and Rigorous Experimental Evaluation: The method is validated across 5 distinct vision backbones (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2) over image classification, image-text retrieval, out-of-distribution transfer datasets, and downstream multimodal LLMs (Qwen3-VL, LLaVA variants) on both image and video understanding tasks.

Strong Low-Bit PTQ Improvements: The gains are particularly notable in aggressive quantization settings (such as W4A4 and W6A6), where activation outliers typically cause baseline PTQ methods to fail severely.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter Search Overhead: RegCache introduces hyperparameters that require tuning per model and bitwidth, specifically the number of register copies and the number of tokens to delete. Although Appendix K demonstrates a label-free reconstruction loss search, establishing a more automated or analytical selection heuristic would improve practical deployment.

Evaluation Predominantly on Base-Scale ViTs: The empirical evaluation focuses almost exclusively on ViT-Base architectures (e.g., CLIP-B/16, SigLIP-B/16, DINOv2-B/14). Evaluating larger encoders commonly used in state-of-the-art VLMs (such as ViT-L/14 or SigLIP-SO400M) would further strengthen claims regarding scalability.

Mixed Results on Self-Supervised Models: On DINOv2 at W8A8, adding RegCache slightly decreases average performance (-0.47%), and requires different insertion strategies (single layer rather than downstream propagation). A clearer theoretical or structural explanation for the divergence between contrastive and self-supervised models would be beneficial.

strengths: Insightful analysis of outlier behavior in vision encoders: The paper provides a clear and compelling empirical characterization of how activation outliers in vision transformers fundamentally differ from LLMs—specifically demonstrating that visual outliers emerge in intermediate layers because identifying semantically uninformative background patches requires multi-layer contextual processing (nicely supported by foreground-only experiments and the tokenization perspective in Appendix M).

Effective and practical training-free formulation: RegCache cleverly exploits the high cross-image cosine similarity (~0.89) of middle-layer sink tokens to precompute a universal KV register cache. Combined with outlier token deletion, it requires no fine-tuning or retraining and adds negligible latency overhead (<1.5% in TensorRT measurements).

Extensive empirical validation: The method is validated across five widely used vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2) and multiple base PTQ algorithms (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, ERQ) down to aggressive low-bit regimes (W4A4). Substantial accuracy recoveries are demonstrated across image classification, image-text retrieval, and downstream VLM benchmarks (Qwen3-VL and LLaVA variants on both image and video understanding tasks).

Strong orthogonality and thorough ablation: The authors show that RegCache functions synergistically as a plug-and-play pre-processing step alongside existing quantization schemes, rotation-based methods (QuaRot), and weight-only quantization (AWQ).
weaknesses: Model scale limited primarily to ViT-Base: The standalone vision encoder experiments focus almost entirely on Base-scale architectures (CLIP-B/16, SigLIP-B/16, DINOv2-B/14). Large pretrained vision backbones (e.g., ViT-L, ViT-H/G) are known to exhibit even more extreme outlier dynamics, and verifying whether universal register caching scales consistently to larger ViT variants would strengthen the empirical foundation.

Hyperparameter search overhead: The curation and caching procedure requires tuning several hyperparameters per model and bitwidth (the register candidate count $k$, prefix duplication factor $\tau$, token deletion count $\tilde{k}$, and target insertion layers). Although Appendix K shows that an unsupervised reconstruction loss can be used, the search still adds calibration complexity.

Divergent behavior on self-supervised models: For DINOv2, the performance improvements are notably less consistent (yielding a minor negative average gap in Tab. 2) and required an ad-hoc modification (inserting prefix tokens only at a single layer rather than propagating to the end). A clearer discussion or systematic handling of self-supervised versus contrastively trained models would be beneficial.

Potential friction with dense prediction pipelines: While Appendix H touches on semantic segmentation using spatial interpolation, dynamic token deletion can disrupt standard rectangular grid layouts and batched dense prediction architectures without custom padding or masking logic.

strengths: Compelling Empirical Insights on ViT Outliers: The paper provides a thorough and convincing analysis distinguishing the behavior of activation outliers in vision encoders from LLMs. Specifically, demonstrating that outliers emerge in intermediate/middle layers rather than early layers—due to continuous visual tokenization needing deeper layers to identify semantically uninformative background patches—is well-motivated and insightful.

Comprehensive and Extensive Experiments: The authors validate RegCache across five diverse vision encoders (CLIP, OpenCLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, DINOv2), five established PTQ algorithms (PTQ4ViT, RepQ-ViT, NoisyQuant, FIMA-Q, ERQ), and multiple bitwidths (W4A4, W6A6, W8A8). The evaluations also extend convincingly to downstream tasks (MS-COCO retrieval, 7 zero-shot classification datasets, ADE20K segmentation) and VLMs (Qwen3-VL 2B/8B, LLaVA-1.5/NeXT) on image and video benchmarks.

Training-Free and Plug-and-Play Integration: RegCache requires zero model fine-tuning or retraining, operating as a lightweight pre-processing/inference add-on with negligible latency overhead (~1% on TensorRT profiling).

Substantial Low-Bit Performance Gains: Activation quantization in extreme low-bit regimes (e.g., W4A4 and W6A6) has historically suffered severe degradation; RegCache brings large and consistent accuracy recoveries across multiple baselines.
weaknesses: Architecture-Dependent Synergy in Ablations: In Table 8, the individual contributions of prefix caching and token deletion vary drastically across model architectures. For SigLIP-B/16, prefix caching alone provides virtually all gains (74.37 vs 69.71 baseline), while token deletion alone severely harms accuracy (42.41). Conversely, for SigLIP2-B/16, token deletion accounts for the vast majority of the gain (69.06 vs 26.04 baseline), while prefix caching alone drops performance (23.82). While the combined system achieves the best score on both, this disparity indicates that the primary failure mode and mitigation mechanism differ significantly across models.

Inference Overhead of Dynamic Token Deletion for Dense Tasks: Dropping tokens dynamically at intermediate layers disrupts regular 2D spatial grid structures. Although Appendix H demonstrates an interpolation workaround for semantic segmentation, this introduces task-specific operational complexity compared to standard dense ViT inference pipelines.

Hyperparameter Search and Tuning: The method relies on several discrete hyperparameters that need tuning per architecture/quantizer pair, such as the prefix layer index, copy factor tau, and deletion count k_tilde. While Appendix K offers a reconstruction-loss alternative, tuning remains empirical and heuristic.

Diminishing Returns on Highly Resilient Models / Higher Bitwidths: In 8-bit quantization with advanced optimizers (e.g., ERQ or FIMA-Q), gains are modest (often <0.5%), and on DINOv2-B/14, RegCache yields minor accuracy degradation (-0.05% to -0.47%).
